title: Not by matted hair (391–400)
hook: not matted hair nor family makes one noble, but truth and goodness; the one who owns nothing and clings to nothing

segments.voice: Yesterday, brahmana, a title earned by conduct, and your line: not by birth. Did you manage one noble thing that nobody found out about? Day two hundred twenty-six.

We all wear badges. Some are literal: a uniform, a lanyard, a ring. Some are subtler: the right sneakers, the reading list on the coffee table, the practice you mention casually at dinner. Spiritual life has its badges too. A string of beads on the wrist, the right vocabulary, a meditation app streak you'd rather people noticed. In the Buddha's India, the badge of a holy man was often his hair, grown long and matted, and a robe of animal skin. Today's verses look straight at the badge. Today: not by matted hair.
screen: `WE ALL WEAR BADGES.` → `SPIRITUAL LIFE HAS THEM TOO.` → `LONG, MATTED HAIR.`

segments.voice: Verse three hundred ninety-three, in Max Müller's English: "A man does not become a Brahmana by his plaited hair, by his family, or by birth; in whom there is truth and righteousness, he is blessed, he is a Brahmana." Plaited, or matted, hair was the sign of a certain kind of ascetic in ancient India, many of them devoted, serious people. The verse isn't mocking them. It's saying the sign isn't the thing. The next verse says it more sharply, speaking straight to someone vain about his look: what use is your matted hair, what use your robe of goatskin? The inside is a tangle, and you're polishing the outside. Then the verses turn to the real thing, and the picture is surprising. The one this chapter honors might wear rags taken from a rubbish heap, be thin enough that you can see the veins, and sit alone in the forest, meditating. No badge at all. One verse even plays with how people addressed each other. Someone with plenty of possessions, the text says, might be called sir, but he isn't a brahmana for that. The brahmana is the one who owns nothing and clings to nothing. Then the portrait keeps filling in. The one who has cut every fetter and trembles at nothing. The one who bears insults, blows and even chains without anger, whose patience is an army. The one free of anger, faithful in duty, keeping the precepts, tamed. This is the fourth time in these weeks that the book has said it: the robe, the shaved head, the gray hair and now the matted hair aren't the point. The heart is.
screen: `NOT BY PLAITED HAIR, FAMILY OR BIRTH.` · `A TANGLE INSIDE, POLISHED OUTSIDE.` · `RAGS, VEINS, ALONE IN THE FOREST.` · `OWNS NOTHING, CLINGS TO NOTHING.` · then, large: `NOT BY THE HAIR.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Think of one badge you wear, spiritual or otherwise. Something you like people to notice about you. It might be small: a phrase you use, a thing you own, a streak you keep. Hold it lightly in your mind. Then imagine setting it down beside you, just for this sit. What's left without it? Breath. A body. Attention. Notice that nothing essential went missing. Rest there, with no badge at all. The bell holds the time.
Not by matted hair. The sign isn't the thing: truth and goodness make one noble, not the look of holiness.
Your line: not by the hair. Today, let go of one badge: do the good thing without mentioning it, or leave the sign at home. Day two hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Buddhist monastics wear a simple robe and shave their heads, and teachers often use these verses to warn that the robe itself is not the practice; the rag-robe ideal lives on in some forest traditions.

match.prompt: match each piece of today's verses.

fork.setup: two people arrive at a monastery: one with long matted hair and a goatskin robe, one in rags, quiet and kind. whom does this chapter call a brahmana?
options: the one with the matted hair.
the one with truth and goodness in them.
fork.reveal: verse 393: not by plaited hair, family or birth; the one in whom there is truth and righteousness is a brahmana.

original.note: Pali jaṭā: matted hair, the sign of some ascetics; verse 393 says it doesn't make one noble.

trapdoor: what you thought: holy people look holy.
what it means: the sign isn't the thing; truth and goodness make one noble, not the look.
what a scholar hears: verse 396 plays on 'bhovadi', one who addresses others as 'bho' (sir), a mark of brahmins in the suttas; the rag-robe (pamsukula) ideal returns in verse 395.

sources.work: The Dhammapada (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 10)
sources.quoted: A man does not become a Brahmana by his plaited hair, by his family, or by birth; in whom there is truth and righteousness, he is blessed, he is a Brahmana.

notes: Check Müller's exact wording of verse 393 in SBE 10 (quoted from memory).
Verse 396's 'bhovadi': rendered 'might be called sir'; the Pali means one who addresses others as 'bho', a way brahmins spoke. Keeper may prefer a different gloss.

The teach says the book made this point for the fourth time, referring to earlier days: 'Not by shaving the head' (208), 'Gray hair isn't wisdom' (207), and the robe in 'Grasp it rightly' (214). Confirm the count reads right.
Matted-hair ascetics (jatila) are described respectfully, as in the canon (e.g. the Kassapa brothers).
